description: To boldly go where no one has gone before.
summary: Clouds hide the Amazon for weeks during the rainy season, and with them two changes that matter: crops emerging and forest torn open by illegal mining. In 2024, our test area in Rondônia, Brazil, went 63 days without a single clear optical image (NASA HLS). Germina uses NISAR, the new NASA-ISRO L-band radar, which works with or without clouds, and turns every pass into a dated record. In the Sararé Indigenous Territory, home of the Nambikwara people and the Brazilian territory with the most illegal-mining alerts in 2025 (Ibama), NISAR shows standing forest returning about twice the radar echo of mining pits, checked against 224 official mining polygons. On farmland, the same echo rose about 4 dB on three real fields when the crop emerged, while control areas stayed flat. Every result shows which NISAR pass it came from and when. The code is open, and the method is built to work wherever NISAR flies.
details:
Our Problem

Clouds delay what we see on the ground.

- In the rainy season, optical satellites lose the ground for weeks. In southern Rondônia, average cloud cover is about 88% in November and December (NASA POWER), and in 2024 our test area went 63 days without a clear image (NASA HLS).

- Brazil's official forest alerts (DETER/INPE) still work, but in cloudy months part of the clearing only shows up the next month.

In Indigenous lands, that delay matters.

- The Sararé Indigenous Territory (67,719 ha, Mato Grosso) is home to the Nambikwara people.

- In 2025, it had the most illegal-mining alerts of any territory in Brazil: 1,814 (Ibama).

- Mining has destroyed 743 ha of native vegetation there and brought mercury into the rivers.

- In March 2026, the federal government launched a major operation to remove the miners. After an operation, the open question is whether each scar recovers or grows again.

On farms, the same gap hurts farmers.

Farmers, banks and insurers need to know if a crop was planted and when it emerged. When the image fails, it falls back on paperwork or a field visit.

 Our solution and how it works

1. NISAR passes over the same area every 12 days, day or night, with or without clouds.

2. It sends a microwave signal and listens to the echo (HV polarization). Standing forest and growing crops return a strong echo; open pits and the ground before the crop return little.

3. Germina measures that echo on every field and every 100 m block, and follows how it changes from pass to pass.

4. Every result is dated. It shows the NISAR pass ID and date it came from, and the app shows where NISAR is right now and when it will pass again.

Results with real NISAR data

All numbers below come from real NISAR L2 GCOV data (provisional, 2026).

Forest vs. mining in the Sararé Indigenous Territory

- We split the territory into 100 m blocks and compared them with the official mining map (DETER/INPE: 211 alerts, 224 mining polygons).

- Standing forest (44,668 blocks): median HV of −10.9 dB.

- Recent mining pits (1,109 blocks): −14.3 dB.

- Older pits (325 blocks): −15.1 dB (pass of 17 Jul 2026, track 132).

- The same pattern repeats on 21 Oct 2026 and on a second track.

- A 3 dB gap means the forest returns about twice the echo of a mining pit.

Crop emergence in Rondônia

- Baseline = median HV before 30 Sep 2026 (about −21 dB).

- A field counts as emerged when the echo rises +1.5 dB above the baseline and the next pass confirms it.

- On three real fields, the echo rose +4.2, +4.2 and +3.8 dB: first detected on 9 Oct and confirmed on 21 Oct. Control areas stayed flat (±0.2 dB).

- The fields look like soybean in optical images, but the crop type and planting date still need field confirmation.

Why it matters for the Amazon and Indigenous lands

  • A dated record every 12 days, even under clouds. After the removal operation, Germina can follow each mapped scar pass by pass and show whether it stays open, grows or starts to recover.
  • Free and open. It runs on public NASA data and open code, so Indigenous organizations, prosecutors and journalists can check the same numbers without paying for imagery.
  • The communities decide. Germina is built to be designed with the people who live there. We want to co-design it with Nambikwara organizations and groups that already work with them, such as OPAN, and we have not started that yet.
  • For farmers in the same region: a record that their crop emerged, even under closed skies, to keep their credit or claim their insurance.
  • For banks and insurers: send people to the field only where the radar did not see the crop emerge. First goal: a pilot with 30 fields and a local credit cooperative.

It works anywhere NISAR flies

Germina needs only two things: an outline (a field, a territory) and NISAR passes, and NISAR covers nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days. The same cloudy season hides farms and forests across the tropics: the Congo Basin, Southeast Asia and India's monsoon. India, NISAR's partner country, already uses satellites in its national crop insurance (PMFBY). Next step: run the same code in another tropical country.

Limitations

  • NISAR data is still provisional (the mission's first year).
  • In the Sararé, we have so far measured the contrast between forest and pits. Following each scar over time is the next step.
  • The radar indicates crop emergence, but the method still needs field validation and calibration with real planting dates. We want to start with Embrapa's experimental field in Vilhena.
  • Radar does not replace field teams or official alerts. It adds a dated record when the sky is closed.
